Active-learning screening baseline

Source: R/core-bench-baseline.R
hr_baseline_ranker.Rd

Simulates prioritised screening over a set where every record's relevance is already known, the way ASReview's simulation mode does: the result shows how much reading a cheap ranker would have saved, which a model screener has to beat.

Usage

hr_baseline_ranker(
  texts,
  labels,
  seed_n = c(1, 1),
  batch = 1,
  model = c("logistic", "naive_bayes"),
  seed = 1,
  lambda = 1,
  min_df = 2,
  max_features = 5000
)

# S3 method for class 'hr_baseline_ranker'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

texts

Character vector, one text per record.

labels

Relevance of each record: logical, or numeric 0 and 1.

seed_n

Number of relevant and irrelevant records known at the start, each at least 1.

batch

Records screened between refits.

model

"logistic" or "naive_bayes".

seed

Seed for the prior records and tie order, on a private random stream.

lambda

Ridge penalty for "logistic".

min_df, max_features

Passed to hr_tfidf().

x

An hr_baseline_ranker.

...

Not used.

Value

An hr_baseline_ranker, a list with order (record positions in screening order), relevant (their labels in that order), curve (a data frame of n_screened, item, relevant, found and recall), n_95, wss_95, random_n_95, prior (the seed records), n_fits, n_total, n_relevant and settings. gr_stop_test() accepts it directly.

Details

Procedure. Under seed, seed_n[1] relevant and seed_n[2] irrelevant records are drawn as the prior knowledge and screened first, in a random order. Then, until every record is screened: fit the model on the records screened so far, score the rest, and screen the batch with the highest predicted probability of relevance (ties broken by a seeded random order). Features are hr_tfidf() over all texts, which uses no labels. Once the last relevant record has been screened, the remaining records are ordered by the last model without refitting, since their order changes no figure reported here.

Models. "logistic" is the ridge logistic regression of hr_baseline_classifier() with penalty lambda, warm-started from the previous fit. "naive_bayes" is multinomial naive Bayes on the tf-idf weights with add-one smoothing (ASReview's default classifier is also multinomial naive Bayes, with alpha = 3.822).

Measures. recall is the share of relevant records found after each screened record. n_95 is the number screened when recall first reaches 0.95 (the position of the ceiling(0.95 R)-th relevant record, R relevant in all), and WSS@95 = (N - n_95) / N - 0.05 (Cohen et al. 2006): the share of records left unread at 95% recall, less the 5% a random order would leave at that recall. random_n_95 is the expected n_95 of a random order, k (N + 1) / (R + 1) with k = ceiling(0.95 R). The seed records count as screened. WSS depends on prevalence, so compare it only between methods on the same set.

The simulation fits one model per batch, so its cost grows with N / batch fits; raise batch for sets of several thousand.

References

Cohen, A. M., Hersh, W. R., Peterson, K. and Yen, P.-Y. (2006). Reducing workload in systematic review preparation using automated citation classification. Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association 13(2), 206-219.

van de Schoot, R. et al. (2021). An open source machine learning framework for efficient and transparent systematic reviews. Nature Machine Intelligence 3, 125-133.

See also

Other baselines: hr_baseline_classifier(), hr_tfidf()

Examples

set.seed(1)
topic <- function(words, n) {
  vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) paste(sample(words, 6, TRUE), collapse = " "), "")
}
texts <- c(topic(c("masks", "infection", "trial", "ward", "virus"), 10),
           topic(c("budget", "policy", "school", "survey", "income"), 50))
labels <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(10, 50))
r <- hr_baseline_ranker(texts, labels)
r
#> <hr_baseline_ranker> logistic, 60 records, 10 relevant, 9 fits
#>   95% recall after 11 records (random order: 55.5 expected)
#>   WSS@95: 0.767
head(r$curve, 12)
#>    n_screened item relevant found recall
#> 1           1    9        1     1    0.1
#> 2           2   14        0     1    0.1
#> 3           3    1        1     2    0.2
#> 4           4    7        1     3    0.3
#> 5           5    5        1     4    0.4
#> 6           6    6        1     5    0.5
#> 7           7    8        1     6    0.6
#> 8           8    2        1     7    0.7
#> 9           9    4        1     8    0.8
#> 10         10    3        1     9    0.9
#> 11         11   10        1    10    1.0
#> 12         12   48        0    10    1.0
